transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
President Trump's returning home from his unprecedented trilateral meeting with his
counterparts from Russia and China, the host.
The meeting on the sidelines of the Apex summit yielded no known major breakthroughs, but
the three nuclear powers issued a joint declaration on peace.
SpaceX officially trading on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT.
The maker of the artificial intelligence chatbot Claude debuted shortly before noon Eastern
at $111.50 a share.
That was more than 30 percent higher than the $83 per share set during its historic
initial public offering.
NPR's John Ruich says it's the highest, the biggest IPO ever.
It beats Elon Musk's SpaceX, which brought in $75 billion when it listed this summer.
Anthropics sold nearly one billion shares and the IPO raised more than $107 billion.
That's a combination of shares offered to the public and other tech companies and others
that the company's founders sold.
The IPO put Anthropics value at around $1.5 trillion, which is stunning if you think about
it.
The company's only five years old.
NPR's John Ruich.
House Democrats have begun laying the groundwork for how they plan to govern in the majority
next year.
That includes rallying behind a leader, and on Wednesday, the caucus overwhelmingly nominated
New York's Hakeem Jeffries to be the next speaker of the House.
Here's NPR's Elena Moore.
Jeffries got 251 yes votes and just 11 no votes in a closed-door caucus meeting.
He's not speaker just yet.
The final vote happens at the start of the new Congress in January.
Jeffries is widely expected to win.
And if he does, he'll make history as the first black lawmaker to serve in the job.
The Democrats are already laying out their agenda for the majority, pledging to lower
costs from the price of gas and groceries to health care and housing affordability,
as well as rooting out alleged corruption within the Trump administration, notably just
hours before the vote Wednesday.
The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee, Robert Garcia, sent document preservation
letters to more than a dozen of President Trump's inner circle.
Elena Moore, NPR News.
The U.N.'s highest court finds Myanmar guilty of committing genocide against its minority
Muslim population, the Rohingya.
More from Terry Schultz.
This case was opened seven years ago when Gambia, a majority Muslim country, accused
Myanmar of intentionally trying to eradicate its Muslim minority population, the Rohingya,
in 2016 and 2017.
Judges at the International Court of Justice, the ICJ, declared Myanmar is guilty on several
counts of genocide.
Here's Judge Yuji Iwasawa, president of the ICJ.
The court finds that Myanmar security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated
widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children.
The court ordered Myanmar to cease any ongoing violation of its obligations.
It's NPR.
JPMorgan Chase is disclosing that third-party vendors may have been targeted in a cyber
attack.
It says there were no disruptions to its services, but hackers are believed to have accessed
certain marketing data held by third parties, which may include some customer names and
email addresses.
JPMorgan Chase and other banks were swept up in recent days in tech outages that led
to some customers complaining they could not access their online accounts.
Tech issues in recent days and weeks also affected the NSA, Apple, Microsoft Outlook
and the FAA, prompting a nationwide ground stop.
Meta has developed a plan to increase teens' use of the online platform Instagram.
Internal documents suggest Meta will build connections with schools across the U.S.,
but NPR's Katie McKee reports experts say the plan makes teens less safe.
Meta called the plan Project Gryffindor.
It encourages students to add school banners to their profiles and use directories to connect
with other classmates.
Meta launched the school partnership program in 2025, nearly 17,000 schools have signed
up.
Publicly, Meta said the program is designed to improve student safety, help schools report
bullying and keep families informed about school activities.
Yet, cybersecurity experts say the program increases teens' vulnerability to scammers
and hackers, who often try to access their connections for blackmail and sextortion schemes.
And experts say the program's student directories will make this easier to do.
Meta disputes his criticisms, saying the program provides meaningful safety protections.
Katie McHugh, NPR News, New York.

topics.text: President Trump returns home after trilateral meeting with Russia and China leaders at Apex summit
SpaceX trades on Nasdaq under symbol ANT
Anthropic debuts on Nasdaq at $111.50 a share, its $107 billion IPO highest ever
House Democrats caucus nominates Hakeem Jeffries for next House speaker, 251-11 vote
Rep. Robert Garcia sends document preservation letters to Trump inner circle
UN International Court of Justice finds Myanmar guilty of genocide against Rohingya
JPMorgan Chase discloses third-party vendors may have been targeted in cyber attack
Recent tech outages affect NSA, Apple, Microsoft Outlook, and FAA prompting nationwide ground stop
Meta's Project Gryffindor plan to boost teen Instagram use through school partnerships criticized as unsafe
